paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Johnson was a mob attack on a Black man in the quarry district north of Lemont, Illinois, reported in a Joliet dispatch dated July 1, 1903. A crowd of nearly 300 Slavs and Poles chased, beat and fired at Johnson after he was found asleep in a woman's bedroom, but he escaped alive. The dispatch credited his survival to his "fleetness of foot" and added that he was later adjudged insane.

Johnson, described in the dispatch as "a half-witted negro," had wandered into one of the houses in the quarry district and gone to sleep in the bedroom of Mrs. Frank S. Zolecki. The neighborhood's residents were described as Poles and Slavs, "none of whom can talk the English language."

When Mrs. Zolecki discovered Johnson she began to scream, and he ran from the house. Poles and Slavs of the district joined the chase, and according to the dispatch a mob of nearly 300 "clamored for the negro's life." In the darkness Johnson climbed a tree, and while the crowd searched for him the limb broke and he fell among them.
In the struggle that followed he was "terribly beaten and maltreated," and members of the crowd fired many shots in his direction. Johnson nonetheless broke away and hid in the high weeds.
When Johnson was found, he was brought to Joliet, adjudged insane and sent to Kankakee. The coverage names no member of the mob and reports no arrests, inquiry or prosecution.

The episode is known from a single Joliet wire dispatch that ran in white papers on July 1, 1903. The Rock Island Argus printed the fuller version on its front page under the headline "Mob Has a Chase After Insane Negro," with a deck that described Johnson as "Found in a House Where He Did Not Belong." The Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican ran a shorter text as "Speed Saved Him," spelling the town "Lamont" and the householder "Zolocki."

Both versions called the mob "infuriated" and stressed that its members could not speak English, while describing Johnson as "half-witted" and the incident as a near-lynching he outran. No Black-press coverage of the attack was found, and no local Joliet or Lemont account appears in the coverage.
